claim: Attack cost is an attacker-side efficiency metric in Cho et al.'s classification.
quote: Attack cost [5], [6], [93], [113], [147]: This measures how much overhead or impact is introduced to attackers to perform their attacks.
locator: Sec. VII-B, p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21)
issue: Cho is cited for its own classification (caption: 'as Cho et al. classify them'), so not secondary.

claim: Defence cost and system performance overhead are defender-side efficiency metrics in Cho et al.'s classification.
quote: System performance [9], [33], [36], [48], [54], [68], [85], [105], [118], [132] [163], [164], [176]: This metric measures how much overhead is introduced to deploy a given MTD
locator: Sec. VII-B, p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21)
issue: Cho lists 'System performance' and 'Defense cost' as two separate defender efficiency metrics; the cell merges them into one entry, which is harmless.

claim: Quality of service is a defender-side efficiency metric in Cho et al.'s classification.
quote: Quality-of-Service (QoS) to users [35], [68], [168]: This metric captures the degree of service quality provided to users while implementing a given MTD technique
locator: Sec. VII-B, p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21)

claim: Return on attack sits in Cho et al.'s attacker-side efficiency class (via the caption 'MTD metrics as Cho et al. classify them').
quote: The MTD efﬁciency from the attacker’s perspective is mainly measured by two types of metrics as above
locator: Sec. VII-B, p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21)
issue: Cho's attacker-side efficiency class holds only 'penalty in attack payoff' and 'attack cost'; RoA (cited to cremonini2005, alavizadeh2022, not Cho) is placed in Cho's grid by this dissertation, and the caption's 'as Cho et al. classify them' covers it only loosely. Caption issue, not a cell defect.

claim: Cho et al. name four MTD evaluation methods: analytical models, simulations, emulations and real testbeds.
quote: we discuss how the performance of MTD techniques have been assessed based on the following evaluation methods: (1) analytical models; (2) simulation models; (3) emulation models; and (4) real testbeds.
locator: Sec. VIII (intro), p. 730 printed (PDF p. 22)

claim: (Uncited neighbour) An analytical model computes the outcome from a probabilistic or graph model of the network, the attacker and MTD.
quote: In probabilistic models, the behaviors of a system, an attacker, and a defender and the interactions between them are described based on probabilistic parameters.
locator: Sec. VIII-A-1/2, p. 730 printed (PDF p. 22)
issue: Cho's two analytical sub-types are probabilistic models and graphical security models (VIII-A-1, VIII-A-2), matching the gloss. The simulation gloss ('runs a program ... over simulated time') and U0220's emulation/testbed glosses are generic definitions Cho does not give; common knowledge, no source needed. The U0218 cite covers the paragraph.

claim: Analytical models are the cheapest of the four evaluation methods to evaluate.
quote: The evaluation of probabilistic models provides insights and lessons based on the observations of general system behaviors with minimum evaluation cost.
locator: Sec. VIII-A-1 Pros and Cons, p. 730 printed (PDF p. 22); also Table VI, p. 732 printed (PDF p. 24), analytical models 'minimum cost', real testbeds 'highest cost among all available evaluation tools' (table is an image, not in the text cache)
issue: Table VI's ranking carries the superlative.

claim: Analytical models are the most abstract of the four evaluation methods.
quote: due to the probabilistic parameterization of all the key system design features, a certain level of simplicity and abstraction is unavoidable
locator: Sec. VIII-A-1 Pros and Cons, p. 730 printed (PDF p. 22); Table VI, p. 732 printed (PDF p. 24)
issue: Cho says abstraction is unavoidable in analytical models but never ranks them 'the most abstract'; Table VI also lists 'a certain level of abstraction/simplicity' as a con of emulation. The superlative is our inference from the ordering. Cho also gives scalability (GSM, SPN) as an analytical con, which the sentence drops (does not change the point).

claim: Emulations and real testbeds are the most realistic evaluation methods.
quote: Emulation models can provide a higher validity than simulation models in the experimental results validated through them.
locator: Sec. VIII-C and VIII-D Pros and Cons, p. 731-732 printed (PDF p. 23-24); Table VI: emulation 'High validity; ... more realistic scenarios', real testbeds 'Highest flexibility and validity ... among all other available evaluation tools'
issue: Cho ranks real testbeds highest and emulation above simulation, so the pair is the realistic end. Cho's word is 'validity'; 'realistic' is its Table VI word for emulation and its VIII-D word for testbeds ('more realistic system environments').

claim: Emulations and real testbeds are hard to scale to large networks.
quote: However, it is difﬁcult to evaluate the MTD techniques in large-scale networks. Most real testbed-based studies have focused on assessing the performance of MTD in small or mid-sized networks.
locator: Sec. VIII-D Pros and Cons, p. 732 printed (PDF p. 24); emulation: Sec. VIII-C, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23), 'making it difﬁcult to evaluate experiments for large-scale networks'

claim: Simulation is the dominant MTD evaluation method.
quote: Most studies evaluating the performance of MTD approaches have been validated based on simulation experiments.
locator: Sec. VIII-B, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23)
issue: 'Most studies' carries 'dominant'. Scope is Cho's 2020 corpus; present tense is acceptable for a survey finding.

claim: Simulation is dominant because it models specific attack behaviours more flexibly than an analytical model.
quote: Compared to analytical models, simulation models have more ﬂexibility in modeling speciﬁc attack behaviors
locator: Sec. VIII-B, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23)
issue: Cho states the two facts side by side (most studies use simulation; simulation is more flexible than analytical models) but never says the flexibility is why simulation dominates. The causal 'because' is ours.
fix_text: "is the dominant evaluation method, because it models" -> "is the dominant evaluation method, and it models"

claim: Simulation results do not transfer directly to a real network, because no simulation fully captures it.
quote: However, the simulation model has its inherent limitations because all possible variables may not be captured due to the nature of existing, uncontrollable uncertainty. Therefore, the lessons obtained from the simulation studies may not be realized in real testbed-based experiments or systems.
locator: Sec. VIII-B Pros and Cons, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23)
issue: Cho hedges twice ('may not be captured', 'may not be realized'); the sentence states it as fact ('do not transfer', 'no simulation fully captures'). 'Directly' softens it but does not restore the hedge.

claim: Cho et al.'s survey finds that MTD attacker models lack properties of an APT attacker.
quote: Smart, intelligent attackers are signiﬁcantly less considered: Most MTD techniques are shufﬂing-based to deal with attacks.
locator: Sec. V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Cho's limitations are framed as missing 'smart, intelligent' / rational, learning attackers, not as missing APT properties; the APT link is ours, via V-A ('More or less, APT attackers show the above features', which covers adaptivity and incentive-driven behaviour but not learning or strategy choice). Cho also hedges ('significantly less considered', 'rarely studied') where the sentence says 'lack'. Cho's own finding, not secondary.

claim: Cho et al. add choice of attack strategy as a property an MTD attacker model needs to model an APT attacker.
quote: few scenarios have considered multiple strategies that can be taken by attackers or defenders.
locator: Sec. V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Cho names the gap (multiple attacker strategies rarely modelled) but as a limitation of attack models in general, never as an APT property. The sentence's frame ('needs ... to model an APT attacker. The two surveys add the other four') attributes the APT link to the surveys.

claim: Cho et al. add cost-benefit reasoning as a property an MTD attacker model needs.
quote: we can consider the attacker to be a rational actor that is sensitive to incentives, such as attack success with minimum cost [52].
locator: Sec. V-A (incentive-driven attackers), p. 721 printed (PDF p. 13); V-D bullet 3, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: V-A ties this characteristic to APT attackers ('More or less, APT attackers show the above features').

claim: Cho et al. add learning and deployment-strategy awareness as properties an MTD attacker model needs.
quote: An attacker has been less considered as a rational decision maker with learning ability: The smart attackers can leverage how MTD works and what side-effect the MTD can introduce.
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 3, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: The properties are Cho's, but as features of 'smart attackers'; Cho does not tie learning or exploiting how MTD works to APT attackers (V-A's APT list is persistent, adaptive, stealthy, incentive-driven). Jalowski may carry the APT link; on Cho alone it is ours.

claim: Cho et al. name three limitations of MTD attacker models.
quote: we can identify the following limitations in the current attack models:
locator: Sec. V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: V-D has exactly three bulleted limitations.

claim: (Uncited neighbour) MTD attacker models lack adaptivity and learning: the attacker follows fixed attack patterns while the defender adapts and learns.
quote: Generally, it is assumed that attackers have certain attack patterns, rather than that they learn and can launch adaptive attacks. Whereas the contrary is true for defenders; they are often permitted to take proactive, adaptive defense actions based on an assumed highly intelligent learning capability.
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 1, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Covered by U0233's cite. 'Generally' dropped, which does not change the point.

claim: (Uncited neighbour) In practice the attacker is often the smarter of the two.
quote: This assumption may not be true; even the attackers are often smarter than the defenders in practice [83].
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 1, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Cho reports this from [83], an Internet Security Threat Report (2015) slideshare page, 'Attackers Are Getting Smarter Than Defenders'. A weak primary; Cho's own hedge 'may not be true' is dropped.

claim: (Uncited neighbour) MTD attacker models lack choice of attack strategy: few evaluations let the attacker choose among several attack strategies.
quote: Unfortunately, most MTD approaches focus on a single or a small set of attacks, and few scenarios have considered multiple strategies that can be taken by attackers or defenders.
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 2, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Covered by U0233's cite.

claim: (Uncited neighbour) MTD attacker models lack cost-benefit reasoning and deployment-strategy awareness: the attacker is seldom modelled as a rational actor, or as one that exploits how the MTD works.
quote: An attacker has been less considered as a rational decision maker with learning ability: The smart attackers can leverage how MTD works and what side-effect the MTD can introduce.
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 3, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Covered by U0233's cite. 'Less considered' -> 'seldom' is close enough.

claim: Choice of attack strategy, defined as choosing among several sequences of techniques toward the same objective, is a property sourced to Cho et al.
quote: For example, the attacker may need to decide which system vulnerability it needs to target while the defender may want to determine which defense mechanism needs to be used
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 2, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Cho's idea is the attacker choosing among 'multiple strategies' (its example: which vulnerability to target); 'sequences of techniques toward the same objective' is our operationalisation, and Cho does not frame it as an APT property (caption: 'needs to model an APT attacker'). Row 3 cites Cho alone, so the APT link rests on our synthesis.

claim: Adaptivity, defined as choosing the next technique in response to an MTD disruption, is a property sourced to Cho et al.
quote: Adaptive attackers: Attackers are adaptive to dynamically changing system conditions and external environmental conditions
locator: Sec. V-A, p. 720 printed (PDF p. 12)
issue: Cho's adaptivity is broader (changing system and environmental conditions, resource management); the row narrows it to MTD disruptions, which is a specialisation, not an overstatement. V-A ties it to APT attackers.

claim: Cost-benefit reasoning, defined as choosing each technique by weighing its cost against its benefit, is a property sourced to Cho et al.
quote: attackers are intelligent enough to execute attacks efﬁciently, such that the attack has a minimal cost but maximal outcome.
locator: Sec. V-A (incentive-driven attackers), p. 721 printed (PDF p. 13)
issue: 'Each technique' is our granularity; the cost-versus-outcome weighing is Cho's own wording.

claim: Learning, defined as keeping patterns observed in past MTD deployments and using them to choose later techniques, is a property sourced to Cho et al.
quote: If attackers are intelligent such that they are able to detect defense patterns by using learning mechanisms (e.g., machine learning or cognitive learning), then they can easily capture what types of MTD techniques are used and what the patterns are to trigger an MTD operation.
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 1, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)

claim: Deployment-strategy awareness, defined as predicting and leveraging which mechanism the deployment strategy deploys next, and when, is a property sourced to Cho et al.
quote: The smart attackers can leverage how MTD works and what side-effect the MTD can introduce. In addition, they can capture the defense patterns for an adaptive MTD
locator: Sec. V-D bullet 3, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15); 'which' and 'when' from bullet 1: 'what types of MTD techniques are used and what the patterns are to trigger an MTD operation'
issue: 'Predicts ... next' extrapolates slightly from Cho's 'capture ... patterns', but the which/when pair maps onto Cho's types/trigger patterns. Cho puts the which/when sentence under the learning limitation, so rows 7 and 8 split one Cho passage.

claim: Two surveys (Cho et al. one of them) find that MTD attacker models lack properties of an APT attacker.
quote: Smart, intelligent attackers are signiﬁcantly less considered: Most MTD techniques are shufﬂing-based to deal with attacks.
locator: Sec. V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: Same as U0226: Cho frames the gaps as missing smart, rational, learning attackers, not APT properties, and hedges ('significantly less considered') where the sentence says 'lack'. The APT framing is our reading.

claim: Cho et al. are the source of the attack success probability (ASP) metric (Table 4.5, 'Source' column).
quote: Attack success probability (ASP) [3], [11], [22], [25], [26], [28], [32], [45], [49], [136], [147], [173]: This metric refers to the probability that attacks are successfully performed.
locator: Sec. VII-A, p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19)
issue: Cho is a survey that collects ASP from twelve primary works (e.g. Al-Shaer et al. [3], Carroll et al. [25]). A 'Source' column reads as origin. Defensible as the definition cite (Cho's own gloss and its finding that ASP is the dominant effectiveness metric), but Table 3.1 also cites evans2011 for ASP, which could be added here.
fix_text: "\citep{cho2020}" -> "\citep{evans2011, cho2020}" (or keep, if the column means the definition followed)

claim: ASP is the share of runs in which the attacker reaches its goal (definition cited to Cho et al.).
quote: the attack success probability (e.g., whether an attacker achieved its goal of a launched attack such as ﬁnding a vulnerable target) is a dominant metric
locator: Sec. VII-A, p. 729 printed (PDF p. 21); definition at p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19): 'the probability that attacks are successfully performed'
issue: Cho defines ASP as a probability that the attacker achieves its goal; 'the share of runs' is our estimator of that probability over simulation runs. The goal part is Cho's, the operationalisation is ours.
fix_text: "ASP is the share of runs in which the attacker reaches its goal \citep{cho2020}:" -> "ASP is the probability that the attacker reaches its goal \citep{cho2020}, estimated as the share of runs in which it does:"

claim: Cho et al. support that the attacker model decides which deployment strategy is optimal.
quote: In addition, if incentives based on rationality are not compatible (e.g., attackers are not stimulated by the incentives), the best strategies derived by the defender may not work for irrational attackers.
locator: Sec. VI-A (disadvantages of game theoretic MTD), p. 725 printed (PDF p. 17)
issue: Cho gives only a narrower, hedged, game-theory-specific version (a strategy derived for a rational attacker 'may not work' for an irrational one). Section 3.2.1 draws the general claim as its own inference ('The attacker model therefore decides ...', uncited there); this sentence attaches [cho2020] directly to that inference.
fix_text: "argued that the attacker model decides which deployment strategy is optimal \citep{cho2020}" -> "argued, from Cho et al.'s survey \citep{cho2020}, that the attacker model decides which deployment strategy is optimal"

claim: Simulation is the dominant evaluation method and models specific attack behaviours flexibly.
quote: Most studies evaluating the performance of MTD approaches have been validated based on simulation experiments. Compared to analytical models, simulation models have more ﬂexibility in modeling speciﬁc attack behaviors
locator: Sec. VIII-B, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23)
issue: No causal 'because' here, unlike U0223.

claim: Simulation results do not transfer directly to a real network.
quote: Therefore, the lessons obtained from the simulation studies may not be realized in real testbed-based experiments or systems.
locator: Sec. VIII-B Pros and Cons, p. 731 printed (PDF p. 23)
issue: Hedge dropped, as in U0224: Cho says lessons 'may not be realized'.
fix_text: "its results do not transfer directly" -> "its results may not transfer"

claim: Game theory is the dominant MTD modelling approach.
quote: game theoretic approaches are dominantly employed in developing MTD.
locator: Sec. VI-D, p. 727 printed (PDF p. 19)
issue: Cho's own trend finding over its 2020 corpus. The rest of the sentence (our three models include none from game theory) is ours.

claim: Cho et al.'s survey finds that MTD attacker models in general lack the properties of an APT attacker (the eight properties).
quote: Persistent attackers: In the existing MTD works, we found that attackers are persistent, not performing a onetime attack (e.g., APT attacks [22], [45], [49], [78]).
locator: Sec. V-A, p. 720 printed (PDF p. 12); compare V-D, p. 723 printed (PDF p. 15)
issue: 'The properties' reads as the eight (or all). Cho's V-D limitations cover adaptivity, learning, choice of strategy, cost-benefit reasoning and deployment-strategy awareness only. Its V-A reports that existing MTD works do model persistent attackers, and stealthy ones ([3], [87]), which cuts against campaign persistence and detection avoidance being lacking 'in general'. The dissertation's own round-47 note says the surveys' evidence covers six of the eight.
fix_text: "lack the properties of an APT attacker" -> "lack several properties of an APT attacker"
